p3-3.a: When a new medicine is tested, patients at hospitals worldwide are randomly assigned to get the medicine or a comparison.|IRT is the system that does that assignment fairly, tells the site which drug kit to give, and makes sure each site always has enough stock by triggering shipments from depots.|It also tracks shipments and supports electronic consent.|Because it affects patient safety and trial results, it is regulated: every change is validated and audited.
p3-3.qa: When a new medicine is tested, patients at hospitals worldwide are randomly assigned to receive it or a comparison treatment. IRT is the system that makes that assignment fairly and secretly, tells the hospital which numbered drug kit to give, and makes sure every hospital always has enough stock by triggering shipments from depots, while tracking those shipments. Because it affects patient safety and trial results, every change is validated and every action is audited.
i: Analogy: a fair lottery plus an automatic stock manager for a global pharmacy chain, where nobody knows who got what.
Blinding: doctors and patients don't know the treatment; kit numbers hide it.
Interactive Response Technology used to mean phone systems (IVRS); now it's web-based.
Regulation: GxP, 21 CFR Part 11 (electronic records and signatures), audit trails.
Shows you understand the business, not just the code.
f: What happens if IRT is down?
Sites can't randomize or dispense, which can delay patient treatment, so availability and support matter.
What is eConsent?
Electronic informed consent: patients review and sign trial consent digitally with an audit trail.
wv: I can explain technical work to non-technical people.

p3-8.a: Why: deployments on on-prem Azure DevOps Server were manual and multi-node, took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people.|What: an MCP server with about 77 tools that exposes build, release and multi-node deployment operations to AI agents.|How: typed tools grouped by builds, releases and deployments, wrapping Azure DevOps Server APIs and our install scripts, with status polling, clear structured outputs and human approval for risky steps; packaged so teammates install and use it.|Impact: deployment time cut from 6 hours to 2, people per deployment from 6 to 1.
p3-8.qa: Deployments on our on-prem Azure DevOps Server were manual and multi-node, took about 6 hours and needed about 6 people. I built the CIRT MCP server: about 77 typed tools for builds, releases and multi-node deployments, wrapping Azure DevOps APIs and our install scripts, with status polling, structured outputs and human approval for risky steps, packaged as a .NET tool. Deployment time fell from 6 hours to 2 and people per deployment from 6 to 1.
i: Why MCP: one server works across Cursor, Claude Code and Copilot; engineers describe intent in plain language.
How: C# MCP SDK, stdio transport, tools grouped by domain, long operations return ids plus status tools.
Safety: each user's own PAT, read vs write tools, confirmations, approvals unchanged, audit log of every call.
Adoption: demo, README with [10] prompts, pairing, feature requests turned into tools.
Measured on [8 vs 8] comparable deployments from release history.
f: What would you do differently?
Involve QA and TechOps earlier and add a central audit store from day one.
Is it still in use?
Yes, most of our team's release deployments run through it.
wv: I find high-leverage problems and solve them end to end.
I measure impact instead of claiming it.

p3-9.a: Situation: before the CIRT MCP server went to the wider team, my lead wanted evidence, not impressions.|Task: compare deployments with and without the tool fairly.|Action: from the Azure DevOps Server release history I took [8] deployments from the [two release cycles] before the tool, using start and end timestamps and the attendee lists of the deployment calls. I compared them with [8] similar deployments over the [next two cycles] that used the tool, on the same environments and node counts ([4 to 6] nodes).|Result: average time fell from about 6 hours to about 2, and people from 6 to 1. Approvals, FV and UAT validation, and decisions when a step fails still need humans.
p3-9.fu: Where do the remaining 2 hours go?::Mostly the real install time on each node, service warm-up, smoke tests and waiting for approvals. The tool removed hand-offs and manual checking, not the work the servers must do.||Was it a fair comparison?::Same environments, similar release sizes and node counts, and the same timestamps source. It is not a lab experiment, but the difference is large and consistent.||What do the other 5 people do now?::They work on their sprint tasks and only join if a step fails and needs their area's expertise.
p3-9.qa: My lead wanted evidence, so I compared [8] deployments from the [two release cycles] before the tool with [8] similar deployments from the [next two cycles] using it, on the same environments and node counts, using Azure DevOps release start and end timestamps and deployment-call attendee lists. Average time fell from about 6 hours to about 2, and people from 6 to 1; approvals and validation still need humans.
i: Like-for-like comparison: same environments and [4 to 6] nodes, similar release size.
Data source was the system of record, not memory or estimates.
Be honest about limits: small sample, some improvement from better scripts too.
Business translation: [about 20 person-hours to 2 per deployment].
f: Could other factors explain the gain?
Some, like script fixes, but the person count dropped because the agent runs the steps one person used to coordinate.
How would you measure it better now?
Log every deployment's start, end and operator automatically through the tool.
wv: I back claims with data and state limitations honestly.

p3-10.a: Designing tool boundaries so the model picks the right tool among about 77: naming, descriptions and schemas mattered more than code.|Long-running operations: deployments take time, so tools start work and return ids, and status tools poll.|On-prem Azure DevOps Server API differences and authentication.|Safety: separating read and write tools and keeping humans in control of production steps.
p3-10.qa: The hardest part was designing tool boundaries so the model reliably chose the right one among about 77: naming, descriptions and schemas mattered more than code. Next were long-running deployments (start returns an id, status tools poll), differences and authentication quirks of on-prem Azure DevOps Server APIs, and keeping humans in control of production steps.
i: Fix for wrong tool choices: verb_noun naming, "use when" in descriptions, enums for environments, removing overlapping tools.
Context budget: summarised outputs instead of raw JSON logs.
On-prem API versions differ from Azure DevOps Services docs; I tested each call against our server.
Safety design: read-only tools first, write tools with confirmation, production via existing approvals.
f: How did you test tool selection?
Ran real prompts from teammates and logged which tools the agent called, then adjusted descriptions.
What failed in early versions?
The agent sometimes polled too aggressively; I added recommended wait times in tool outputs.
wv: I solve ambiguous design problems by iterating with real users.

p3-11.a: Situation: the first version ran from my local clone. Teammates had to build it from source, and their versions drifted.|Task: make it install in minutes and update easily.|Action: I packaged the CIRT MCP server as a .NET global tool (PackAsTool) built on the C# MCP SDK. Its own pipeline publishes it to our internal Azure Artifacts feed on every tag. Teammates run dotnet tool install -g and add one entry to the MCP config of Cursor or Claude Code using the stdio transport. The Azure DevOps Server URL and each person's personal access token come from environment variables, never from files in the repo. Releases use semantic versions with release notes, dotnet tool update -g upgrades it, and a health_check tool confirms connectivity.|Result: setup went from [about an hour of building from source] to [about 10 minutes], and everyone stays on the same version.
p3-11.fu: Why a .NET tool and not an npm package or Docker image?::The team already has the .NET SDK, and the deployment logic and Azure DevOps client code were in C#. A global tool is one command to install, with no extra runtime.||Why stdio and not HTTP?::Each engineer runs it locally with their own credentials, so stdio is simplest and keeps permissions per person. HTTP would need a hosted service with its own authentication.||How do you handle breaking changes to tools?::Add new tools or optional parameters instead of changing existing ones, bump the major version when something must break, and note it in the release notes.
p3-11.qa: The first version ran from my clone and teammates' copies drifted, so I packaged the CIRT MCP server as a .NET global tool published to our internal Azure Artifacts feed by its own pipeline on every tag. Teammates run dotnet tool install -g and add one entry to their Cursor or Claude Code MCP config; the server URL and each person's PAT come from environment variables. Setup went from [about an hour] to [about 10 minutes], with everyone on the same version.
i: PackAsTool and ToolCommandName in the csproj; semantic versions and release notes.
dotnet tool update -g for upgrades; health_check tool confirms connectivity and permissions.
No secrets in config files or the repo.
f: Why not a Docker image?
A global tool is simpler for developers' machines and starts instantly over stdio.
How do you ship a breaking change?
New major version with release notes, and keep old tool names working for a release.
wv: I think about the user experience of internal tools, not just features.

p3-12.a: IRT exchanges data files with external vendors over SFTP.|I owned a component supporting three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, behind one common object-oriented abstraction (connect, upload, download, list, delete).|A factory picks the provider from configuration, so callers never change; shared retry, logging and error mapping live in a base class.|I released the Rebex provider to production for vendor data exchange.
p3-12.qa: IRT exchanges data files with external vendors over SFTP. I owned a component that supports three providers, ComponentPro, SSH.NET and Rebex, behind one ISftpClient abstraction (connect, upload, download, list, delete); a factory picks the provider from per-vendor configuration so callers never change, and a base class holds shared retry, logging and error mapping. I released the Rebex provider to production.
i: Patterns: strategy + factory + template method; adapter per library.
Error mapping turns library-specific exceptions into our own (AuthFailed, HostKeyMismatch, Timeout).
Host key pinning per vendor; keys and passwords from Secrets Manager.
Atomic upload: write to a temp name then rename so vendors never pick up partial files.
Integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH server] in CI.
f: Why not just pick one library?
Vendors differ and libraries evolve; the abstraction let us switch per vendor safely (next question has the story).
How do you handle large files?
Stream them without loading into memory, with resumable transfers where supported.
wv: I design for change so new requirements don't ripple through callers.

p3-13.a: Situation: ComponentPro was the original SFTP library. [Its updates had slowed and its licence renewal was under review], and in [2024] [a depot vendor hardened their SFTP server and disabled older algorithms such as ssh-rsa with SHA-1], so our connection to them started failing. SSH.NET had been added earlier as a free option, but we wanted commercial support for a regulated product.|Task: choose a long-term provider without rewriting any caller.|Action: I compared the three on modern algorithm support (rsa-sha2-256/512, curve25519, AES-GCM), commercial support and patch frequency, licence cost, and behaviour against each vendor's test server. I built the Rebex provider behind the existing ISftpClient interface and ran parallel test transfers against vendor test endpoints.|Result: we chose Rebex and moved vendors to it one at a time through configuration, keeping the other providers as a fallback during the transition.
p3-13.fu: Why not just use SSH.NET, since it is free?::It is a good library, but for vendor data exchange in a GxP product we valued a vendor support contract and predictable patch releases. The abstraction keeps SSH.NET available if that changes.||How do you verify the server's identity?::We pin each vendor's host key fingerprint in configuration and reject the connection if it does not match, which prevents man-in-the-middle attacks.||Will you remove the old providers?::Once every vendor has run on Rebex for [a few release cycles], yes. Removing unused code reduces the security and licence surface.
p3-13.qa: ComponentPro was the original library, but its updates had slowed and in [2024] a depot vendor disabled older algorithms like ssh-rsa with SHA-1, breaking our connection; SSH.NET was free but we wanted commercial support for a regulated product. I compared all three on modern algorithm support, support and patching, licence cost and behaviour against each vendor's test server, built a Rebex provider behind the existing interface, and we moved vendors to it one at a time by configuration.
i: Algorithm terms worth knowing: rsa-sha2-256/512 host keys, curve25519-sha256 key exchange, aes256-gcm ciphers.
Evaluation matrix made the decision objective and reviewable.
Keeping other providers as fallback reduced risk during migration.
Lesson: abstraction paid off; no caller code changed.
f: Isn't three libraries over-engineering?
Temporarily, for migration and fallback; the plan was to retire ComponentPro once all vendors moved.
What did Rebex cost?
[A commercial licence], justified by support and regulated-product needs.
wv: I make technical decisions with clear criteria and evidence.

p3-14.a: Situation: after choosing Rebex, we had to switch production vendor transfers to it without breaking [daily] file exchanges.|Task: I owned the implementation and the production release.|Action: I implemented it behind the existing interface, with unit tests using mocks and integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH test server] in CI. I tested key exchange, host key checks, a [500 MB] file, timeouts and reconnects. It went through FV, TechOps and UAT with documented evidence. In production I enabled it by configuration for [one low-volume vendor] for [two weeks], watched the transfer logs and alerts, then switched the rest.|Result: [no failed transfers were caused by the switch], and we never needed the fallback.
p3-14.fu: How do you test SFTP in CI?::Start a disposable SFTP server container in the pipeline, run upload, download, list and delete tests against it, then throw it away.||How is the Rebex licence key handled?::Stored as a secret (pipeline secret or secrets store) and injected at runtime, never committed to the repo.
p3-14.qa: I implemented Rebex behind the existing interface with unit tests and integration tests against [a containerised OpenSSH server] in CI (key exchange, host keys, a [500 MB] file, timeouts, reconnects), took it through FV, TechOps and UAT with evidence, then enabled it in production by configuration for [one low-volume vendor] for [two weeks] while watching logs and alerts before switching the rest. No failed transfers were caused by the switch.
i: Canary by configuration: a per-vendor Provider setting, no redeploy needed to switch or roll back.
Observability: transfer success and duration metrics per provider, alerts on failures.
Rollback plan: flip config back to the previous provider.
Same pattern as feature flags: deploy dark, enable gradually.
f: What would make you roll back?
Any failed transfer or auth error attributable to the new provider.
How did you get evidence for GxP?
Test reports from FV and UAT with transfer logs attached to the change record.
wv: I release risky changes gradually with a rollback ready.

p3-15.a: Situation: study setup teams entered [site records and site-level settings] one by one. A large study with [300+] sites took [two to three days], and typing mistakes caused rework.|Task: build a bulk import, used by a regulated product and now live in production.|Action: the API accepts a CSV of up to [5 MB, about 10,000 rows] and parses it as a stream with CsvHelper. Validation runs in stages: headers, data types, mandatory fields, duplicates inside the file and against the database, then business rules such as valid country and depot. With the BA we chose all-or-nothing saving, because a half-imported study is risky in GxP. A preview step shows every error (row, column, reason) and lets the user download it. On confirm, rows are saved in batches inside one transaction, with an audit entry per record carrying the import id and user. A file hash blocks importing the same file twice. Unit tests cover each rule, and Playwright end-to-end tests cover the upload flow.|Result: live in production. A [300-site] setup went from [days to under an hour], and errors are caught before anything is saved.
p3-15.fu: Why all-or-nothing instead of saving the valid rows?::A partly configured study is hard to audit and easy to forget about. The preview step gives users the friendliness of partial import (they see every error at once) without the risk.||What about large files and timeouts?::Parsing is streamed, and the file size is capped. For much bigger files I would move the import to a background job that returns 202 and a job id.||How do you prevent CSV injection in the error report?::Cells starting with =, +, - or @ are prefixed with a quote when exported, so Excel will not run them as formulas.
p3-15.qa: Study setup teams typed [300+] site records by hand over [two to three days]. I built a CSV import (up to [5 MB, ~10,000 rows]) that streams with CsvHelper, validates in stages (headers, types, mandatory fields, duplicates in file and database, business rules), shows a preview of every error, then saves all-or-nothing in batches inside one transaction with an audit entry per record and a file hash to block re-imports. It is live in production and a [300-site] setup takes [under an hour].
i: Staged validation fails fast on structural errors before expensive database checks.
Duplicate checks with one set-based query instead of per-row lookups.
Error report downloadable as CSV with row, column and reason.
[Concurrency limit 2 per user] and request size limits protect the system.
Tests: unit test per rule, Playwright end-to-end for upload, preview and confirm.
f: Why InvariantCulture?
So numbers and dates parse the same on every server regardless of locale.
How did you handle a 10,000-row transaction?
Batched inserts inside one transaction with a reasonable timeout; tested at maximum size.
wv: I deliver features end to end, from requirements to production.

p3-16.a: Situation: studies are configured in a lower environment and then transferred onwards, for example from UAT to production. In [2024] a manual check caught a near-miss: a transfer was about to run against a target study that already had randomized subjects.|Task: turn the manual checklist into a rule enforced by the system.|Action: before any transfer, the backend guard runs five checks. (1) Target study status: block if it is live with enrolled or randomized subjects or dispensed kits. (2) Version compatibility: source and target application and configuration schema versions must match. (3) Direction: only allowed paths, for example lower to higher environment, never overwriting production from production. (4) No other transfer in progress for that study, enforced with a lock. (5) The user has the required role and gives a change request reference. Each failure returns a specific reason, and every attempt, blocked or allowed, goes into the audit trail. Each rule has unit tests, plus integration tests.|Result: released in [2025]. It blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts in the first months, each with a clear message, and validators liked that the rule is testable and auditable.
p3-16.fu: Can an admin override the guard?::Not in the application. A real exception goes through a change request and a separate controlled procedure, which keeps the audit story clean.||Why enforce it in the backend and not just the UI?::Transfers can also be triggered by scripts and APIs. Only the backend sees every path.||What about two transfers racing?::The checks and the lock run in one transaction, so a second transfer for the same study waits or is rejected.
p3-16.qa: In [2024] a manual check caught a study transfer about to overwrite a target study that already had randomized subjects. I replaced the checklist with a backend guard that runs five checks before any transfer: target study status (block if live with subjects or dispensed kits), version compatibility, allowed direction, no transfer already in progress (lock), and user role plus a change request reference; each failure returns a clear reason and every attempt is audited.
i: Fail-closed: if any check can't be evaluated, block.
Lock with sp_getapplock or a unique "transfer in progress" row to prevent races.
Specific error codes help users fix the issue instead of raising tickets.
Released in [2025]; blocked [a handful of] unsafe attempts in its first months.
f: Why check in the backend, not just the UI?
The UI can be bypassed; the API is the real boundary.
Can an admin override it?
[Only with a documented emergency process and dual approval], audited.
wv: I turn near-misses into system-enforced safeguards.

Verification: version endpoint on every node, health checks, key business smoke tests.
Config and database changes reviewed separately (the ValidateOnStart lesson).

f: What's the most common release problem?
Environment configuration differences, which is why we validate options at startup and use checklists.
How do you handle a late feature?
Agree with the product owner to move it to the next release rather than risk validation.

p3-18.a: Situation: [one evening in mid-2024] a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while a [large vendor shipment-status file] was loading. The broker blocked publishers and dropped some connections. For [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates from the vendor integration service never reached the shipment service, so [some sites saw stale shipment statuses]. Randomization and dispensing were not affected.|Task: I was on the support rotation, so I had to restore the flow, find the root cause and prevent a repeat.|Action: a CloudWatch alarm on consumer inactivity fired. Grafana showed the integration service publishing normally while the incoming rate on the shipments queue had dropped to zero. The RabbitMQ management UI showed the memory alarm and blocked connections. The app logs had no errors because we published with BasicPublish and no confirms, so messages lost during connection resets were invisible. I scaled out consumers to drain the backlog and replayed the missed window by re-processing the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert status by shipment id. The permanent fix: publisher confirms with tracking of unconfirmed messages, retry with backoff on nack or timeout, persistent messages on durable queues, consumers that ack only after committing, and alerts on nacks, memory alarms and blocked connections. I wrote the post-mortem.|Result: the replay recovered all [about 1,200] updates the same evening. In the [12 months] since there has been no silent message loss, and a later broker restart produced [a few dozen] nacks that were retried automatically and showed up in alerts.
p3-18.fu: Why did the broker block publishers?::When RabbitMQ crosses its memory high watermark it raises a memory alarm and blocks publishing connections until memory falls, to protect itself. Slow consumers plus a burst of messages caused it.||Did confirms slow publishing?::We track confirms asynchronously instead of waiting after each message, so throughput dropped only about [5 percent].||How did you know the replay would not create duplicates?::Consumers upsert by shipment id and ignore a status older than the one stored, so processing a message twice leaves the same result.

p3-18.qa: In [mid-2024] a RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark during a [large vendor shipment-status file], blocked publishers and dropped connections, and for [about 40 minutes] status updates silently never reached the shipment service. On support, I confirmed it through CloudWatch, Grafana and the management UI, drained the backlog, replayed the missed window from vendor files (safe because consumers upsert), then fixed the root cause with publisher confirms, retries, memory tuning and alerts. All [about 1,200] updates were recovered that evening, with no silent loss since.
i: Root cause vs trigger: the file was the trigger; publishing without confirms was the root cause.
Prevention: confirms with async tracking, alarms on memory, blocked connections and zero incoming rate, consumer scaling on queue depth.
Blameless post-mortem shared with the team.
Code for confirms is in Part 2, Q40.
f: Why didn't anyone notice sooner?
There were no errors to alert on; we added a rate-drop alert.
Did patients get affected?
No; randomization and dispensing were unaffected, only shipment status display was delayed.
wv: I stay calm under pressure and restore service first.
I fix causes, not just symptoms, and share lessons.

p3-19.a: Token-based logout: made sure logging out actually invalidates the session or tokens instead of leaving them usable until expiry.|SSO cookie 'header too long' failures: reduced cookie or header size so SSO requests stopped failing.|Reverse tabnabbing: added rel=noopener noreferrer to external links opened in new tabs.|Each went through code review, testing and the regulated release process.
p3-19.qa: I delivered three security fixes in [2024]: real token-based logout (shorter access tokens, refresh-token revocation and a jti denylist in ElastiCache), SSO "request header too long" failures (auth ticket moved to a server-side ITicketStore, cookie from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB]) and reverse tabnabbing ([about 40] links fixed with rel=noopener noreferrer plus an ESLint rule). Each had tests and went through review and the regulated release process.
i: Pattern: fix the root cause and add a guard so it cannot come back (tests, lint rule).
Map to OWASP: broken authentication/session management, security misconfiguration, client-side risks.
Performance impact measured: denylist check about [1 ms] per request.
Detailed stories: Part 2 Q48–50.
f: Which was hardest?
The SSO cookie issue, because it only affected some users and needed a pattern to reproduce.
How do you find security issues proactively?
SonarQube, dependency scanning, security reviews and reading OWASP guidance.
wv: I take security seriously and verify fixes with automation.

SharePoint Server Object Model and CSOM/REST APIs; PowerShell for administration.

p3-21.a: Node.js/TypeScript example: [a build-log summariser service for the MCP platform]. It pulls logs from Azure DevOps Server, finds the failed step and the key error lines, and returns a short structured summary the agent can show.|Python FastAPI example: [a vendor file pre-validation service] that checks incoming shipment files against a schema (Pydantic models) before the .NET import runs, returning 422 with the exact problems.|Python Flask example: [a small internal endpoint exposing release and deployment status] for team dashboards.|Same standards everywhere: REST contracts, structured logs to CloudWatch, Jest or pytest tests, Docker images and the same Azure DevOps pipeline template. p3-21.fu: Why Node for the log summariser?::It is I/O-bound (fetch logs, parse text, return JSON), Node handles that well, and the TypeScript MCP and HTTP libraries made it quick to build.||Why validate vendor files in Python before the .NET import?::Pydantic gave quick, readable schema validation that the integration team could maintain. Rejecting bad files early keeps the core .NET import simpler.
p3-21.qa: I pick the language by fit: Node.js/TypeScript for I/O-heavy glue such as [a build-log summariser for the MCP platform], Python FastAPI for [a vendor file pre-validation service using Pydantic schemas] and Flask for [a small release-status endpoint], and .NET for core domain services. All follow the same standards: REST contracts, structured logs to CloudWatch, Jest or pytest tests, Docker images and the same Azure DevOps pipeline template.
i: Shared standards make polyglot services operable: same health endpoints, logging fields, correlation id header.
FastAPI returns 422 with field-level problems automatically from Pydantic validation.
Node async I/O suits log fetching and parsing.
Avoid polyglot sprawl: only where a language is a clear fit.
f: Why not write everything in .NET?
We could; for small tools the Node and Python ecosystems were faster to build with, and the team knew them.
How do they share auth?
All validate the same JWTs from the identity provider.
wv: I'm pragmatic with technology choices and consistent with standards.

p3-22.qa: I build responsive, reusable React/TypeScript components and work on Angular modules in the IRT UI, fixed UI security issues such as reverse tabnabbing, and write Playwright and Cucumber end-to-end tests for user flows, connected to APIs I built, so I understand the full request path.

Practices: typed props, hooks, accessibility (labels, keyboard), memoisation only when measured.
Data fetching with loading and error states; API errors mapped from ProblemDetails.
Playwright tests use stable selectors (data-testid, roles).
f: React or Angular?
Both in IRT; I'm stronger in React for new components and maintain Angular modules.
How do you test React components?
React Testing Library for components, Playwright for flows.

p3-23.a: Check dashboards: is it all endpoints or one, since when, did a release or traffic spike happen?|Look at latency by dependency: database, downstream services, CPU/memory, thread pool, connection pool.|Use logs and traces with correlation ids to find the slow step; check slow queries and execution plans.|Mitigate (scale out, rollback, cache), then fix the root cause and add an alert.|Situation: one morning in [March 2025] the shipments API's p95 latency jumped from [about 200 ms to about 3 seconds] during the European peak, with no release that day.|Task: I picked up the alert and had to restore normal latency.|Action: Grafana showed database latency up and CPU normal. CloudWatch logs, filtered by correlation id, pointed to one query. Query Store showed its plan had changed after an overnight statistics update, a parameter-sniffing case where a plan compiled for a tiny study was reused for large ones. I forced the previous good plan in Query Store within [about 20 minutes], then rewrote the query and added a covering index so any plan performs well.|Result: latency returned to [about 200 ms] and has not recurred, and I added a p95 alarm on that endpoint.
p3-23.fu: What is plan forcing in Query Store?::Query Store keeps the history of plans per query. You can force a known good plan so the optimizer uses it, which is a fast, reversible mitigation.||Why not just restart the service?::The problem was in the database plan, not the app, so a restart would not have helped. Evidence first, then action.
p3-23.qa: I check scope and timing on dashboards (one endpoint or all, since when, release or traffic change), then latency by dependency, then traces and logs by correlation id to find the slow step, mitigate, fix the cause and add an alert. In [March 2025] the shipments API p95 jumped from [about 200 ms to about 3 s] with no release; Query Store showed a plan change after a statistics update (parameter sniffing). I forced the good plan to restore service, then fixed the query and index permanently.
i: Immediate mitigation: Query Store plan forcing or sp_recompile, then a durable fix (OPTION (RECOMPILE) or OPTIMIZE FOR, better index, or .NET-side query shape).
Check thread pool starvation (sync over async), connection pool exhaustion and GC as other causes.
Tools: Grafana, CloudWatch Logs Insights, X-Ray/OpenTelemetry traces, dotnet-counters.
Add a p95 latency alert per endpoint and a Query Store regression review.
f: What is parameter sniffing?
SQL Server compiles a plan for the first parameter values and reuses it, which can be bad for very different values.
How do you spot thread pool starvation?
dotnet-counters shows thread pool queue length growing and thread count climbing slowly.
wv: I diagnose systematically from symptoms to cause instead of guessing.

p3-24.a: Confirm with metrics that memory grows steadily, not just GC behaviour.|Take memory dumps (dotnet-dump, dotnet-gcdump) at two points and compare the biggest growing object types.|Common causes: static caches without limits, event handlers not unsubscribed, undisposed HttpClient/streams, singletons holding scoped objects.|Fix, load test, and add memory alarms.|Situation: an ECS worker service's memory grew by [about 150 MB a day], and tasks were killed for running out of memory every [about 3 days].|Task: find the leak and stop the restarts.|Action: I took dotnet-gcdump snapshots a few hours apart and compared them. The growth was in a static ConcurrentDictionary that cached study configuration per study and version with no eviction. I replaced it with IMemoryCache with a size limit and a [30-minute] sliding expiration, then ran an overnight load test.|Result: memory stays flat at [about 350 MB], and I added a CloudWatch alarm at [80 percent] of the task's memory.
p3-24.fu: gcdump vs a full memory dump?::A gcdump captures only the managed heap graph, so it is small and safe to take in production. A full dump has everything (including possibly sensitive data) and is much bigger.||Why do static caches leak?::A static field lives for the whole process, so anything added and never removed stays in memory forever.
p3-24.qa: An ECS worker grew [about 150 MB a day] and was OOM-killed every [about 3 days]. I took dotnet-gcdump snapshots hours apart, found a static ConcurrentDictionary caching study configuration per version with no eviction, replaced it with a size-limited IMemoryCache with a [30-minute] sliding expiry, and load tested overnight; memory now stays flat.
i: Tools: dotnet-counters (GC heap size, gen 2 count), dotnet-gcdump for managed heap diff, dotnet-dump for full analysis with SOS (gcroot to find what holds objects).
Common leaks: unbounded static caches, event handlers not unsubscribed, timers, captured closures, singletons holding scoped services, new HttpClient per call (socket exhaustion).
IMemoryCache with SizeLimit requires Size on every entry.
Alert on memory trend, not just the limit.
c:
services.AddMemoryCache(o => o.SizeLimit = 1_000);
cache.Set(key, config, new MemoryCacheEntryOptions { Size = 1, SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30) });
f: Server GC vs workstation GC?
Server GC uses more memory per core for throughput; containers with limits may prefer DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit or workstation/DATAS settings.
What is DATAS?
Dynamic adaptation to application sizes, on by default for Server GC since .NET 9, adjusting heap count to reduce memory.
wv: I use the right diagnostic tools instead of guessing.

p3-25.a: Decide fast: if impact is high, roll back to the previous tagged release.|Look at error logs for the new exception and the endpoints affected.|Check what changed: code, config, database migration, infrastructure.|Fix forward with tests or re-release; write up the cause and add a test or check to the pipeline.|Situation: after a release to [UAT], 5xx errors on one API rose to [about 8 percent].|Task: as release owner, restore the environment and fix the cause.|Action: the logs showed a configuration-binding exception because a new required setting existed in appsettings but not in the UAT environment's parameters. I rolled back within [15 minutes], added the setting, and changed the options to use ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting now fails at startup (the health check fails and the deployment stops) instead of on live requests. I also added a configuration item to the release checklist.|Result: the next-day re-release was clean, and this class of error now stops the deployment instead of reaching users.
p3-25.fu: Why roll back before fixing?::Rollback is fast and known to work. Investigating while users or testers are blocked costs more than a redeploy later.||Why does ValidateOnStart help?::It validates configuration when the app starts, so a broken config makes the deployment fail visibly instead of producing 500s later.
p3-25.qa: Decide fast: if impact is high, roll back to the previous tagged release, then find the cause from logs and the change list and fix forward. After a [UAT] release, 5xx rose to [about 8 percent] because a new required setting was missing from UAT parameters; I rolled back in [15 minutes], added the setting, and switched the options to ValidateOnStart so missing config now fails at startup and stops the deployment instead of failing live requests.
i: Rollback first, investigate second, when users are affected.
ValidateDataAnnotations plus ValidateOnStart (IOptions validation) turns config errors into deploy-time failures.
Readiness checks stop traffic to an instance that fails to start.
Added a configuration item to the release checklist.
f: Why not fix forward immediately?
Rollback is faster and safer when the cause isn't yet certain.
How would canary deploys help?
A small share of traffic would show the errors before full rollout.
wv: I reduce impact first, then make the failure impossible next time.

p3-26.a: Trace one message by id: was it published, did the broker accept it, is it in a queue, DLQ, or was it consumed?|Check publisher confirms, queue depths, consumer errors and acks.|Check for consumers acking before processing, or exceptions swallowed.|Fix the gap and add monitoring on queue depth and DLQ.|Situation: in [validation] testers reported that [a few] kit-assignment notification messages went missing now and then.|Task: find where they were lost.|Action: I traced message ids. They were published, confirmed by the broker and delivered, but the consumer used autoAck=true, so when processing threw a transient database timeout the message was already gone. I switched to manual ack after the database commit, added a retry policy of [3] attempts with backoff, then a dead-letter queue with an alert.|Result: no more missing messages, and [two] messages that later reached the DLQ were replayed after the cause was fixed.
p3-26.fu: autoAck vs manual ack?::With autoAck the broker deletes the message as soon as it is delivered. With manual ack it waits until the consumer confirms success, so a crash or exception means redelivery.||What is a poison message and how do you handle it?::A message that always fails. Limit retries, then move it to the DLQ so it does not block the queue, and alert someone.
p3-26.qa: I trace one message by id through each hop: published, confirmed, queued, delivered, acked, processed. In [validation], kit-assignment notifications occasionally vanished; they were delivered, but the consumer used autoAck=true, so when processing hit a transient database timeout the message was already gone. I switched to manual ack after commit, added [3] retries with backoff and a DLQ with an alert.
i: Ack after the side effect commits, never before.
Prefetch (BasicQos) limits unacked messages per consumer.
DLQ alert and replay tool for poison or exhausted messages.
Idempotent handler because redelivery can now happen.
f: Why requeue false?
Requeue true can loop forever; dead-lettering to a retry queue with delay is controlled.
What does prefetch do?
Limits how many unacked messages the broker pushes to a consumer.
wv: I follow evidence hop by hop rather than assuming where data is lost.

p3-27.a: Stop the rollout so nodes do not drift further apart.|Compare the failing node: logs from Ansible/scripts, disk space, permissions, service state, config, versions.|Fix and rerun the idempotent step on that node, then verify all nodes are on the same version.|Add a pre-check for that condition to the automation or MCP tool.|Situation: a UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5] because the service would not start.|Task: finish the deployment and stop it happening again.|Action: I paused the rollout. The Ansible output showed the files copied but the service failed to start, and the node's event log showed the disk was [98 percent] full from old release folders and unrotated logs. I removed old releases (keeping the last [2]), re-ran the idempotent step on that node, and confirmed all nodes reported the same version. I then added a prerequisite-check tool to the CIRT MCP server (disk space, service state) and a cleanup step in the scripts.|Result: the deployment finished [about 45 minutes] later, and it has not recurred.
p3-27.fu: Why pause the rollout?::To avoid nodes running different versions, which is harder to support and to validate.||Why can you safely re-run the step?::The install steps are idempotent: they check the current state and only change what differs.
p3-27.qa: Stop the rollout so nodes don't drift, compare the failing node (logs, disk, permissions, service state, config), fix, rerun the idempotent step on that node and verify all nodes report the same version. A UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5] because the disk was [98 percent] full from old releases and logs; I cleaned up (keeping the last [2] releases), reran, verified versions and added a prerequisite-check tool to the CIRT MCP server (disk space, service account, ports) that runs before every deployment.
i: Idempotent steps make reruns safe.
Log rotation and release retention added to the playbook.
Pre-checks shift failures left, before any node changes.
f: Why stop the rollout?
Mixed versions across nodes can break behaviour and complicate rollback.
How do you verify versions?
A version endpoint or file on each node, checked by a tool.
wv: I fix the incident and then automate the check that would have caught it.

p3-28.a: Capture deadlock graphs from system_health extended events.|Identify the queries and resources involved; often a new query or missing index causing scans.|Fix access order, shorten transactions, add the index, consider RCSI.|Add safe retry for deadlock victims.|Situation: after a release, deadlock errors (1205) appeared [about 20 times a day] on inventory updates during kit assignment.|Task: find the cause and remove it.|Action: the system_health deadlock graph showed kit assignment updating Inventory then Shipment, while the resupply job updated Shipment then Inventory, the opposite order. A missing index on Inventory (SiteId, Status) also caused scans and wider locks. I changed the resupply job to the same table order, added the index, shortened the transactions, and added retry for error 1205 (EF Core EnableRetryOnFailure).|Result: deadlocks fell to [about one a week or fewer], and the occasional victim is retried automatically.
p3-28.fu: Why does access order matter?::If every transaction locks tables in the same order, no cycle of waiting can form, so no deadlock.||Is retry alone enough?::No. Retry hides symptoms; fixing the order and the index removes the cause, and retry handles the rare leftover.
p3-28.qa: I capture deadlock graphs from the system_health Extended Events session, find the queries and resources, and fix access order, missing indexes and long transactions. After a release, kit assignment updated Inventory then Shipment while the resupply job did Shipment then Inventory, and a missing index on Inventory (SiteId, Status) caused scans; I aligned the order, added the index, shortened transactions and added retry for error 1205. Deadlocks fell from [about 20 a day] to [about one a week or fewer].
i: Deadlock = cycle of locks; SQL Server kills the cheapest victim (error 1205).
Fixes: consistent access order, covering indexes to reduce lock footprint, short transactions, RCSI to stop readers blocking writers.
EF Core EnableRetryOnFailure retries transient errors including deadlocks; needs execution strategy for user transactions.
c:
SELECT XEvent.query('(event/data/value/deadlock)[1]') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM (SELECT CAST(target_data AS XML) td FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets t
      JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions s ON s.address = t.event_session_address
      WHERE s.name = 'system_health' AND t.target_name = 'ring_buffer') d
CROSS APPLY td.nodes('RingBufferTarget/event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]') AS x(XEvent);
f: Deadlock vs blocking?
Blocking waits until the lock is released; a deadlock is a cycle that never resolves without a victim.
What is RCSI?
Read Committed Snapshot Isolation: readers see the last committed version instead of waiting on writers.
wv: I read the evidence (deadlock graphs) and fix design causes, not just add retries.

p3-29.a: Check our job logs: did the upload run, which provider, any errors or retries?|Verify on the server: file present, size, name, path, permissions; check host key or credential changes.|Re-send if safe (idempotent naming) and confirm with the vendor.|Add alerts for failed transfers and a confirmation step if missing.|Situation: [one Monday] a depot vendor said our daily order file had not arrived.|Task: get the orders to them quickly and find out why.|Action: our job logs showed a successful upload to the /outbound folder, but over the weekend the vendor had moved their pickup folder to [/inbound/irt], announced in an email to a different team. I confirmed the file was in the old folder, re-sent it to the new path with the same file name (the vendor de-duplicates by name), and confirmed with them. I then added a post-upload check that lists the remote folder, alerts on failed transfers, and a change process for vendor connection settings.|Result: the vendor processed the orders [the same morning], with no shipment delay.
p3-29.fu: How do you make a re-send safe?::Deterministic file names and vendor-side de-duplication, so sending the same file twice cannot create duplicate orders.||How do you prevent it next time?::Vendor connection details are changed only through a tracked change, with a test transfer before go-live.
p3-29.qa: I check our job logs, verify on the server (file, size, path, permissions, keys), re-send safely and confirm with the vendor. [One Monday] a depot vendor said our order file hadn't arrived; logs showed a successful upload, but the vendor had moved their pickup folder to [/inbound/irt], announced to another team. I re-sent to the new path with the same name (they dedupe by name), then added a post-upload remote listing check, failed-transfer alerts and [a shared integration contact list] so changes reach us.
i: Evidence first: our logs proved the upload, avoiding blame.
Idempotent naming makes re-sends safe.
Post-upload verification closes the loop.
Communication fix as important as the technical one.
f: What if the logs showed a failure?
Check credentials, host key changes and network, fix, re-send and alert.
How do vendors confirm receipt?
[Some send acknowledgement files, which we now monitor].
wv: I solve the people-and-process part, not just the code.

p3-30.a: `kubectl describe pod` for events: image pull errors, OOMKilled, failed probes.|`kubectl logs --previous` for the app's startup exception.|Check config and secrets, resource limits, and whether liveness probes kill a slow-starting app.|Fix and redeploy; add a startup probe if needed.|Situation: a new version of a Node.js tooling service went into CrashLoopBackOff in the [dev] Kubernetes cluster.|Task: get it healthy and fix the deployment template.|Action: kubectl describe showed liveness probe failures. kubectl logs --previous showed the app needed [about 40 seconds] to warm up (loading configuration and a cache), while the liveness probe started after [10 seconds] and killed it. I added a startupProbe allowing [60 seconds] and made part of the warm-up lazy.|Result: the pods became healthy, and I updated the service template so other services get a startup probe by default.
p3-30.fu: Why a startup probe instead of a longer liveness delay?::A startup probe protects only the start. Liveness can then stay strict, so a hung container is still restarted quickly later.||Liveness vs readiness?::Readiness failure removes the pod from traffic; liveness failure restarts it.

p3-30.qa: I run kubectl describe pod for events (image pull, OOMKilled, probe failures) and kubectl logs --previous for the crash, then check config, secrets, limits and probes. A new Node.js tooling service in [dev] crash-looped because warm-up took [about 40 seconds] while liveness started after [10 seconds] and killed it; I added a startupProbe allowing [60 seconds], made part of the warm-up lazy and updated the service template so all services get a startup probe.
i: CrashLoopBackOff = container keeps exiting; Kubernetes backs off restarts up to 5 minutes.
Exit code 137 = killed (often OOM); 1 = app error; check `lastState.terminated.reason`.
Ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug) help with minimal images.
c:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 12      # up to 60 s to start
f: What does --previous show?
Logs of the last terminated container instance, where the crash happened.
ImagePullBackOff?
The image or tag is wrong or registry credentials are missing.
wv: I fix the template so the whole team benefits.

p3-31.a: Check CloudWatch logs and duration metrics: always or only on cold start?|Find the slow call: VPC networking/NAT, database connections, downstream APIs.|Increase memory (more CPU too), reuse connections, add timeouts, or move long work to a queue or ECS.|Set alarms on errors and duration.|Situation: a Lambda processing DynamoDB stream events for [shipment notifications] started timing out at [30 seconds] as volume grew.|Task: stop the timeouts without losing events.|Action: CloudWatch showed timeouts mostly on large batches, and the logs showed an HTTP client created on every invocation and a slow downstream API called with no timeout. I moved the client outside the handler, set a [5-second] HTTP timeout with retry, reduced the batch size from [100 to 25], enabled ReportBatchItemFailures so only failed records are retried, and raised memory from [512 MB to 1 GB].|Result: p99 duration is about [4 seconds], with no timeouts since.
p3-31.fu: What does ReportBatchItemFailures do?::The function returns the ids of failed records, and Lambda retries only those instead of the whole batch, which avoids reprocessing and endless loops.||Why does more memory help?::Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory, so more memory also means faster code and TLS setup.
p3-31.qa: I check whether timeouts happen always or on cold starts and find the slow call. A DynamoDB-stream Lambda for [shipment notifications] timed out at [30 s] as volume grew: an HttpClient was created per invocation and a slow downstream API had no timeout. I moved the client outside the handler, set a [5-second] timeout with retry, cut batch size from [100 to 25], enabled ReportBatchItemFailures so only failed records retry, and raised memory from [512 MB to 1 GB].
i: Partial batch responses avoid reprocessing whole batches and endless retries.
Bisect on error and maximum retry attempts plus an on-failure destination prevent stuck shards.
More memory also gives more CPU.
Long work belongs in queues or ECS, not one Lambda call.
f: Why is a per-invocation HttpClient bad?
Each creates new connections and TLS handshakes, slowing calls and exhausting sockets.
What happens on a stream batch failure without partial responses?
The whole batch is retried, blocking the shard until success or expiry.
wv: I tune systematically and protect against data loss while fixing performance.

p3-32.a: Find the pattern: which users, browsers, apps, times; check whether those users have many groups or claims.|Inspect the request: cookie and header sizes, token expiry, clock skew, cookie domain/path conflicts.|Check server and load balancer header limits and auth logs.|This is how 'header too long' issues show up; fix the cause (smaller cookies, server-side session) rather than only raising limits.|Situation: in [2024] we had [about 30] tickets over [two weeks], mostly from study managers with many study groups, about 400 errors right after SSO login.|Task: find the pattern and fix the cause.|Action: I reproduced it with a test user in many groups. The chunked auth cookie held every claim, about [13 KB], and with other cookies the header passed the [16 KB] IIS/http.sys limit. I moved the auth ticket to a server-side ITicketStore and loaded permissions per request with caching.|Result: the cookie shrank to [under 1 KB], the tickets stopped, and a regression test now covers a user in [200+] groups.
p3-32.fu: How did you reproduce it?::Created a test user, added them to many groups until the failure appeared, and measured the Cookie header in browser dev tools.||Why did only some users fail?::Cookie size grows with the number of groups and claims, so only users above a certain number of groups crossed the limit.
p3-32.qa: I look for the pattern (which users, browsers, apps, times) and inspect cookies, header sizes, token expiry, clock skew and domain conflicts. In [2024], [about 30] tickets in [two weeks] came mostly from study managers in many groups getting 400 after SSO; the chunked auth cookie held every claim ([about 13 KB]) and with other cookies passed the [16 KB] limit. Moving the ticket to a server-side ITicketStore with cached per-request permissions shrank it to under 1 KB and stopped the tickets.
i: "Random" issues usually have a hidden common factor; find it in the data.
Other causes of random logout: clock skew on token validation, cookies scoped to the wrong domain, data protection keys not shared across instances.
Data protection keys must be persisted and shared (e.g. Redis or S3) when running several instances, or cookies fail to decrypt.
f: Why would logins fail after scaling out?
Each instance had its own data protection keys, so cookies from one couldn't be read by another.
How do you handle clock skew?
Sync clocks and allow a small ClockSkew in token validation (default 5 minutes).
wv: I find patterns in messy support data.

p3-33.a: Look at what failed: new bugs, vulnerabilities, coverage on new code, duplication.|Fix real issues; add missing tests; never mark true issues as false positives to pass.|If it is a genuine false positive, document and get it reviewed.|Talk to the release owner early if it threatens the date.|Situation: [two days] before code freeze, the gate failed: coverage on new code was [68 percent] against an [80 percent] threshold, and SonarQube flagged a hard-coded test connection string as a vulnerability.|Task: get the gate green honestly without slipping the release.|Action: I moved the connection string to user secrets and a pipeline variable, spent [about half a day] writing the missing tests for new validator branches, and updated the release owner that morning.|Result: the gate was green the next day with no date slip and no suppressed issues.
p3-33.fu: Is a coverage target meaningful?::It is a floor, not a goal. Meaningful tests on new logic matter more than the number, but the gate stops untested code slipping in.||What about false positives?::Mark them only with a written reason and a reviewer's agreement, never just to pass.
p3-33.qa: I look at exactly what failed, fix real issues, add missing tests, and never mark true issues as false positives. [Two days] before code freeze, coverage on new code was [68 percent] against [80 percent] and a hard-coded test connection string was flagged; I moved it to user secrets and a pipeline variable, wrote the missing validator tests in [about half a day] and told the release owner that morning. The gate was green next day with no date slip.
i: "Clean as you code": the gate focuses on new code quality.
False positives are documented and reviewed, not silently suppressed.
Communicate early when dates are at risk.
f: Is 80 percent coverage meaningful?
It's a guard, not a goal; meaningful assertions on important branches matter more.
Who can change the gate?
[The quality owner, through a reviewed change], not individual developers.
wv: I hold quality standards even under deadline pressure.

p3-34.a: Look for environment differences: time zone, culture, file paths, OS (Linux agents), env variables.|Check test order dependence and shared static state; xUnit runs test classes in parallel.|Check timing assumptions and async code without awaits.|Reproduce with the same container or agent image.|Situation: a date-formatting unit test passed on my Windows laptop but failed on the Linux build agent.|Task: make it reliable everywhere.|Action: the test expected a dd/MM/yyyy string, but the agent ran with a different culture (en-US). The code used the current culture implicitly. I changed it to format with an explicit culture where a fixed format is required, and made the test set its culture explicitly. I reproduced and verified it in the same .NET SDK container image the agent uses.|Result: the test is stable, and I now run tests in the SDK container before pushing changes that depend on culture or time zone.
p3-34.fu: How do you prevent this class of bug?::Pass CultureInfo explicitly for parsing and formatting, inject time through TimeProvider, and run tests in the same container as CI.||What else commonly differs between local and CI?::File path separators and case sensitivity on Linux, environment variables, parallel test execution and time zones.
p3-34.qa: I look for environment differences (culture, time zone, paths, OS, variables), test order and shared state, and timing assumptions. A date-format test passed on my Windows laptop but failed on the Linux agent because the code used the current culture implicitly; I formatted with an explicit culture, set culture in the test, and verified in the same .NET SDK container the agent uses.
i: Linux is case-sensitive for paths; use Path.Combine.
xUnit runs test classes in parallel; shared static state causes flaky tests.
Time: inject TimeProvider instead of DateTime.Now.
Invariant globalization mode in containers can change culture behaviour.
f: How do you find order-dependent tests?
Run them in random order or individually and see which fail.
What is InvariantGlobalization?
A setting that removes culture data (ICU) from the app, so all cultures behave as invariant.
wv: I make tests deterministic instead of retrying flaky ones.

p3-35.a: Read it critically and check APIs against official docs.|Build it, run tests, add a test for the new behaviour.|Run SonarQube and security checks; look for hallucinated packages or methods.|If still unsure, ask a colleague to review; never merge code you cannot explain.|Situation: Copilot suggested a retry policy for our Azure DevOps API client that retried every failure, including the POST that creates a release.|Task: decide whether to accept it.|Action: I noticed that retrying a non-idempotent POST after a timeout could create duplicate releases. I checked the API docs, limited retries to GET calls and transient status codes (408, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff, and added a unit test proving that a POST is not retried.|Result: the client is resilient without risking duplicate releases, and I shared the example with the team as a reminder to review AI output.
p3-35.fu: What else do you check in AI-generated code?::Hallucinated APIs or packages, missing authorization checks, swallowed exceptions, sync-over-async, and secrets or PHI in logs.||Do you tell the team about such catches?::Yes, short examples in team chat help everyone review AI output better.
p3-35.qa: I read it critically, check APIs against docs, build, test and add tests, run scans, and never merge code I can't explain. Copilot once suggested a retry policy that retried every failure, including the POST that creates a release; retrying a non-idempotent POST after a timeout could create duplicate releases, so I limited retries to GETs and transient codes (408, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff and added a unit test proving POSTs aren't retried.
i: Idempotency matters for retries: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST isn't unless it uses an idempotency key.
.NET 8 resilience handler can disable retries for unsafe methods (DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods).
Shared the example with the team as a review reminder.
f: How do you make a POST safe to retry?
Send an idempotency key the server deduplicates on.
What does the standard resilience handler include?
Rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker and attempt timeout.
wv: I use AI as a helper and stay accountable for correctness.

p3-36.a: Situation: one or two lines of context.|Task: what you were responsible for.|Action: what you did, in first person, with technical detail (this is the longest part).|Result: the outcome with real numbers where you have them, plus what you learned.

End with a lesson or what changed afterwards (STAR-L).
Story bank: MCP server, RabbitMQ outage, CSV import, security fixes, mistake (time-zone bug), disagreement (all-or-nothing), mentoring.
f: What if you don't have numbers?
Use concrete before/after facts (tickets stopped, release on time) and be honest.
How many stories should you prepare?
Eight to ten strong ones that cover leadership, conflict, failure, delivery and technical depth.
wv: I communicate clearly and stay concise.

p3-38.a: Situation: [mid-2024], a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory alarm, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates silently stopped reaching the shipment service.|Task: as the person on support, restore the flow and find the cause.|Action: I used CloudWatch and Grafana to see that publishing looked normal while the queue received nothing, found the memory alarm and blocked connections in RabbitMQ, and realised publishes had no confirms. p3-38.fu: How did you communicate during the incident?::Short updates every [15 minutes] in the incident channel: impact, what we knew, next step, and an all-clear with a summary at the end.||What went into the post-mortem?::Timeline, root cause (no publisher confirms), why monitoring missed it, the fix, and action items: confirms, alerts on nacks and memory alarms, and a replay runbook.

No errors anywhere; I had to reason from metrics that something was missing.

p3-40.a: Situation: in [2023] I changed the date filter in a shipment report API and tested it only with dates in my local time zone (IST). FV testers found that shipments created near midnight UTC appeared on the wrong day for [US sites].|Task: it was my bug, and it had to be fixed before UAT.|Action: I owned it in stand-up. The cause was comparing local DateTime values instead of UTC DateTimeOffset. I changed the code to store and compare in UTC and convert to each site's time zone only for display. I added unit tests for several time zones using a fake clock (TimeProvider), and added a time-zone item to my pull-request checklist.|Result: fixed within [a day], caught in FV rather than production, and I have not shipped a time-zone bug since.
p3-40.fu: What is TimeProvider?::A .NET 8 abstraction for the current time. Injecting it lets tests control the clock instead of depending on the machine's time and time zone.||Why is it fine that FV found it?::That is what validation is for. The real failure would have been reaching production, and the fix made sure the same class of bug is now tested automatically.
p3-40.qa: In [2023] I changed a shipment report date filter and tested only in IST; FV found shipments near midnight UTC appearing on the wrong day for [US sites]. I owned it in stand-up, fixed it to store and compare in UTC DateTimeOffset and convert to each site's time zone only for display, added unit tests for several zones using a fake TimeProvider, and added a time-zone item to my PR checklist. It was fixed within [a day], caught before UAT.
i: Pick a real mistake with low but real impact; show ownership and learning.
Technical lesson: never compare local DateTime values across zones; use TimeZoneInfo for site display.
Testing lesson: inject TimeProvider; test edge times around midnight and DST changes.
f: Why DateTimeOffset?
It carries the offset, so the exact instant is unambiguous.
Why did testing in IST miss it?
IST is UTC+5:30, so the midnight UTC edge falls mid-morning locally and looked normal.
wv: I own my mistakes openly and build habits so they don't repeat.

Who did you check priorities with?
My lead and the release manager.
wv: I create structure and direction when there is none.

p3-48.a: Situation: teammates kept using the manual deployment process even after the CIRT MCP server worked, and I had no authority to mandate it.|Task: win adoption on merit.|Action: I ran a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, made it one command to install, wrote [10] example prompts, paired with the first [4] engineers, and added the tools they asked for.|Result: within [about two months] most of our team's deployments ran through it, with 1 person instead of 6.
p3-48.fu: Who was hardest to convince?::The people closest to production releases, who rightly worried about risk. Human approvals and per-user permissions addressed that.||What would you do if adoption had stalled?::Ask the non-users directly what blocks them and fix that, rather than pushing harder.
p3-48.qa: Teammates kept the manual process and I had no authority to mandate the CIRT MCP server, so I won adoption on merit: a [30-minute] live demo on a real UAT deployment, a one-command install, [10] example prompts, pairing with the first [4] engineers and adding tools they asked for. Within [about two months] most deployments used it, with 1 person instead of 6.
i: Influence = make it easy, safe and visibly valuable.
Addressed concerns directly (permissions, approvals, logs).
Early adopters became advocates.
f: What if someone still refused?
Fine; I'd understand why and fix it if it's a real gap.
How did leadership respond?
[My manager presented the results in the department review].
wv: I lead through credibility and empathy, not authority.

p3-49.a: Situation: in [2023] my lead told me my pull requests were too large ([1,500+ lines]) and slow to review, which held the team up.|Task: change how I deliver code.|Action: I asked for examples, then split my work into smaller pull requests (under [400] lines) with clear descriptions, merging behind feature flags where needed. I asked reviewers after a few weeks whether it had helped.|Result: review turnaround fell from [two to three days] to [usually the same day], and my lead mentioned the change in my appraisal.
p3-49.fu: How do you react to feedback you disagree with?::Ask for the reasoning and examples first. Often there is context I missed, and if I still disagree I explain why with data.||How do you give feedback?::Specific, kind and actionable, with the reason and a suggestion, and privately for anything sensitive.
p3-49.qa: In [2023] my lead said my PRs ([1,500+ lines]) were too big and slow to review. I asked for examples, split work into PRs under [400] lines with clear descriptions, used feature flags where needed, and checked with reviewers after a few weeks. Review turnaround dropped from [two to three days] to [usually the same day], and my lead noted it in my appraisal.
i: Receive feedback without defending; ask for specifics.
Act quickly and visibly, then close the loop.
Small PRs also reduce defects and merge conflicts.
f: How do you give feedback to others?
Specific, timely, kind and actionable, in private for anything sensitive.
Have you received feedback you disagreed with?
Yes; I ask for examples, share my view, and look for the part that's true.
wv: I welcome feedback and change my behaviour quickly.

p3-50.a: PI planning (SAFe): teams plan the next program increment (several sprints), align on objectives and dependencies.|Grooming/refinement: clarify stories, acceptance criteria, estimate.|Sprint planning, daily stand-up, sprint review/demo, retrospective.|I take part in all of these in a ~100-member engineering team.
