p3-50.qa: In SAFe PI planning, teams plan the next program increment (several sprints), align objectives and map dependencies; refinement (grooming) clarifies stories, acceptance criteria and estimates; and each sprint has planning, daily stand-ups, a review/demo and a retrospective. I take part in all of these in our ~100-member engineering organisation.
i: PI planning outputs: team PI objectives, a program board with dependencies, risks ROAMed (resolved, owned, accepted, mitigated).
Refinement with BA and QA ensures testable acceptance criteria (important in GxP).
Demos: I demoed the MCP server increments in sprint demos.
Retros: one concrete improvement action per sprint.
f: What is ROAM?
Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated: how PI risks are categorised.
What makes a good retro?
Safe discussion and one or two actions that actually get done.
wv: I work well in structured agile processes at scale.

p3-51.a: Break stories into tasks; estimate relatively with story points.|Include testing, reviews, validation evidence and release work, not just coding.|Call out unknowns and add spikes.|Use past velocity to check commitments.
p3-51.qa: I break stories into tasks and estimate relatively in story points, including testing, reviews, validation evidence and release work, not just coding; I call out unknowns and add spikes, and check commitments against past velocity.
i: Planning poker exposes different assumptions; discuss the high and low estimates.
Spikes timebox research to reduce uncertainty.
In GxP, validation documentation can be a big share of effort.
Re-estimate or split if a story grows.
f: Points vs hours?
Points measure relative complexity and avoid false precision; hours suit task-level tracking.
What if you're behind?
Say so early with options: cut scope, get help or move the date.
wv: I give realistic estimates and flag risk early.

p3-52.a: Clarify impact and deadlines with the product owner or lead.|Production and patient-safety issues first, then committed sprint goals, then improvements.|Communicate trade-offs openly and early.|Automate repeated work so it stops being urgent.
p3-52.qa: I clarify impact and deadlines with the product owner or lead, handle production and patient-safety issues first, then committed sprint goals, then improvements, communicate trade-offs openly and early, and automate repeated work so it stops being urgent.
i: Frameworks: impact vs effort, Eisenhower matrix.
Make the trade-off visible: "If I do X now, Y slips by two days".
Automation example: MCP server ended many urgent deployment calls.
f: Two managers give conflicting priorities?
Bring them together or escalate to the person who owns priorities.
How do you protect focus time?
Block time for deep work and batch interruptions.
wv: I make priorities explicit and keep stakeholders informed.

p3-53.a: Involve them early in grooming to agree acceptance criteria.|Provide test data, automated tests (Playwright, Cucumber) and clear release notes.|Fix defects quickly and explain root causes.|In GxP, their sign-off is part of the definition of done.
p3-53.qa: I involve QA and validation early in refinement to agree testable acceptance criteria, provide test data, automated tests (Playwright, Cucumber) and clear release notes, fix defects quickly with root-cause explanations, and treat their sign-off as part of done, because in GxP it is.
i: Shared understanding: walk through features with QA before they test.
Traceability: requirements linked to tests and evidence.
Respect: QA findings are help, not criticism.
f: How do you handle a defect found late?
Assess risk with QA and the product owner, fix or document a deviation.
Do developers write automated tests?
Yes, unit and integration, and contribute to end-to-end suites.
wv: I see QA as partners in quality.

p3-54.a: Code reviewed and merged; unit and integration tests pass.|SonarQube gate green; documentation and release notes updated.|Deployed and verified in the test environment; acceptance criteria met.|In regulated work, validation evidence captured.
p3-54.qa: Done means code reviewed and merged, unit and integration tests passing, SonarQube gate green, documentation and release notes updated, deployed and verified in the test environment with acceptance criteria met, and, in regulated work, validation evidence captured.
i: A shared DoD prevents "done but not really" work.
Includes non-functionals: logging, metrics, security checks.
Feature flags: done can mean deployed dark.
f: DoD vs acceptance criteria?
DoD applies to every story; acceptance criteria are specific to one story.
Who owns the DoD?
The team, agreed with the product owner and quality.
wv: I care about finished, shippable work, not just coded work.

p3-55.a: Strong .NET backend and API engineering across a full lifecycle, including releases.|Ownership: I solve problems end to end, like the MCP server and production RCAs.|Using AI tools responsibly to multiply team productivity.|Give one example per strength.
p3-55.qa: My strengths are strong .NET backend and API engineering across the full lifecycle including releases, ownership (I solve problems end to end, like the MCP server and production RCAs), and using AI tools responsibly to multiply team productivity.
i: Give one example per strength: CSV import (lifecycle), RabbitMQ RCA (ownership), MCP adoption (AI multiplier).
Choose strengths that match the job description.
Keep it factual, not boastful.
f: Which strength matters most for this role?
[Link to the JD, e.g. API design and ownership of production services].
What do colleagues say about you?
[That I'm the person they go to for release and deployment problems].
wv: I know my strengths and can prove them.

p3-56.a: Pick a real, non-critical weakness and how you manage it.|Example: I used to take on too much myself (I solely authored the MCP server); now I share design early and delegate.|Or: public speaking in large forums, improving through sprint demos.|Show progress.
p3-56.qa: I used to take on too much myself, for example solely authoring the MCP server for a long time; now I share designs early, write things down and delegate parts so the work isn't dependent on me. It improves both speed and the team's ownership.
i: Real, non-fatal weakness with a concrete improvement and evidence.
Evidence: teammates now contribute tools; [two contributors added features in 2025].
Alternative: speaking in large forums, improving through sprint demos.
f: How do you know it's improving?
Others now contribute and maintain parts of the tool.
Why is it a problem?
It creates a single point of failure and limits others' growth.
wv: I'm self-aware and actively improving.

p3-57.a: I have grown a lot in 4+ years at IQVIA and want a senior backend/API role with bigger design ownership.|I want to work on larger-scale systems and keep applying AI-assisted engineering.|Stay positive about the current employer.|Connect to what this company does.
p3-57.qa: I've grown a lot in 4+ years at IQVIA and now want a senior backend role with bigger design ownership, larger-scale systems and continued AI-assisted engineering, which is what this role offers.
i: Positive, forward-looking; never criticise the current employer.
Link specifically to the new company's product and scale.
Avoid: salary as the headline reason, complaints about managers, or "boredom"; interviewers read these as flight risk.
f: Is it about money?
Compensation matters, but scope and growth are the main reasons.
Would a counter-offer keep you?
I'm looking for scope that my current role can't provide right now.
wv: I'm motivated by growth and impact.

p3-58.a: I bring 5.5 years of .NET backend experience in a regulated, high-quality environment.|I work across .NET, Node, Python, React and AWS, so I can own services end to end.|I have proven automation impact: 6-hour deployments down to 2, 6 people down to 1.|Close by matching to their job description.
p3-58.qa: I bring 5.5 years of .NET backend experience in a regulated, quality-first environment, I work across .NET, Node, Python, React and AWS so I can own services end to end, and I've proven automation impact: deployments from 6 hours to 2 and 6 people to 1. [Then match two or three points to their job description.]
i: Structure: skills match, proof, attitude.
Mention reliability under pressure (production RCAs) and team multiplier (mentoring, adoption).
Close with a one-line summary they'll remember: "I ship reliable .NET services and make teams faster, with numbers to prove it."
f: What would you do in the first 90 days?
Learn the system and people, fix something small, then take ownership of a service or improvement.
What's the gap you'd need to close?
[Their specific domain or a tech I haven't used], which I learn fast.
wv: I connect my experience directly to their needs.

p3-59.a: Leading the design of backend systems as a senior or staff/lead engineer.|Mentoring a team and shaping engineering practices, including AI-assisted development.|Growing with the company's platform.|Keep it ambitious but realistic.
p3-59.qa: In five years I see myself leading the design of backend systems as a senior or staff/lead engineer, mentoring a team, shaping engineering practices including AI-assisted development, and growing with the company's platform.
i: Ambitious but realistic, aligned with the company's career paths.
Show you plan to stay and grow.
Tie the five-year picture to their career ladder (senior → staff/lead) so it sounds like a plan inside their company, not elsewhere.
f: Management or technical track?
Technical leadership first; open to people leadership later.
What skills will you build?
System design at scale, architecture influence and mentoring.
wv: I have a clear growth direction.

p3-60.a: Research the market range for senior backend roles in Bengaluru.|Give a range based on your current CTC, experience and the role's scope; say you are flexible for the right role.|Ask about the full package (bonus, benefits, learning budget).|Use your real numbers; never invent offers.
p3-60.qa: I research the market range for senior backend roles in Bengaluru, give a range based on my current CTC, experience and the role's scope, say I'm flexible for the right role, and ask about the full package. I use real numbers and never invent offers.
i: Let them share the band first if possible.
Anchor slightly above target; know your walk-away number.
Consider total compensation: fixed, variable, ESOPs, benefits, learning budget.
f: What if they ask for current CTC?
Share honestly or say you'd prefer to discuss the role's range.
Can you accept lower?
For the right scope, within reason.
wv: I negotiate professionally and honestly.

p3-61.a: State your real notice period.|Mention if buyout or early release is possible.|Show commitment to a clean handover.|Be honest; do not over-promise.
p3-61.qa: I state my real notice period, mention whether buyout or early release is possible, and commit to a clean handover.
i: Never promise an early date you can't guarantee.
Handover plan: documentation, knowledge transfer for the MCP server and release duties.
If asked to "join next week", say you'll ask about early release but won't leave your team without a handover; that integrity is a positive signal.
f: Can you join in 30 days?
[Answer honestly based on your contract].
What will you hand over?
My services, the MCP server and release integration duties with docs.
wv: I'm honest and responsible to both employers.

p3-62.a: Research their product, tech stack and engineering blog.|Link your experience: .NET microservices, AWS, messaging, regulated quality, AI tooling.|Mention a specific thing you admire.|Show long-term interest.
p3-62.qa: [Research their product, stack and engineering blog, then] link my experience (.NET microservices, AWS, messaging, regulated quality, AI tooling) to what they build, mention one specific thing I admire, and show long-term interest.
i: Specific beats generic: name a product, talk, blog post or tech choice.
Connect to their challenges (scale, reliability, compliance).
Mention something current: a recent product launch, engineering blog post or open-source project of theirs, and how your work relates.
f: What do you know about our stack?
[Prepare two or three facts from their site or job description].
What would you contribute first?
[A matching strength, e.g. reliability and deployment automation].
wv: I do my homework and think about fit.

p3-63.a: State it plainly (67.7 percent) without apologising.|Point to what you have built since: production services, the MCP platform, release ownership.|Show continuous learning (new stacks, AI tooling).|Interviewers care more about 5.5 years of results.
p3-63.qa: My B.Tech aggregate is 67.7 percent. I focus on what I've built since: production services, the MCP platform and release ownership over 5.5 years, plus continuous learning.
i: State it plainly without apology or excuses.
Move quickly to evidence of ability.
If pressed, add one concrete learning habit (e.g. building the MCP prototype from the spec in a week) to show ability beyond grades.
f: Why wasn't it higher?
[One honest sentence, e.g. I focused more on projects than exams], then move on.
What have you learned since?
Cloud, distributed systems, AI tooling and regulated delivery.
wv: I'm comfortable with facts and focus on results.

p3-64.a: What does success look like in the first 90 days?|How are services deployed and monitored; what does on-call look like?|How does the team use AI coding tools?|What are the biggest technical challenges in the next year?
p3-64.qa: I ask what success looks like in the first 90 days, how services are deployed and monitored and what on-call looks like, how the team uses AI coding tools, and the biggest technical challenges in the next year.
i: Also: team structure, code review culture, how decisions are made, growth path to senior/staff.
Avoid asking about things easily found online.
Questions show interest and help you judge fit.
f: Should you ask about salary in the first round?
Usually let HR raise it.
How many questions?
Two or three good ones.
wv: I'm evaluating fit thoughtfully, not just seeking any job.
